chapters.title: Control Valve Specifications for Maintenance
chapters.summary: The specifications a technician reads before touching a valve: the P&ID as a work-scoping map, ASME pressure/temperature class, and ANSI/FCI seat-leakage class.
objectives: Identify critical control components in a P&ID drawing/diagram
Define ASME body class
Define the difference between ANSI/FCI leakage classes I through VI

modules.title: Reading a Valve's Specifications
modules.objective: Read a control valve's duty from its paperwork — locate the valve and its work scope on the P&ID, read the ASME pressure/temperature class off the nameplate, and state the shutoff its ANSI/FCI seat-leakage class allows.

keyConcepts.t: A P&ID is the map of the process. Before touching a valve, use it to scope the job — the control valve and its immediate connections, staying between the flanges, not the whole loop.
On the P&ID the control valve is one tagged symbol; on the bench it is an assembly — actuator on top, then the bonnet, then the valve body between the pipe flanges.
A valve body's pressure rating is not a single number — it falls as temperature rises. The ASME class (150, 300, 600, 900, 1500) names a rating curve, not a fixed pressure.

The pressure–temperature table (ASME B16.34) gives the working pressure for a class, body material, and service temperature — read the class and material off the nameplate, then look up the temperature and watch the number drop down the column.
"Shut off" is not zero flow. ANSI/FCI 70-2 (harmonised with IEC 60534-4) defines six seat-leakage classes and the factory leak-tests the valve to one of them. Class I means no test was done.

The classes tighten by roughly a factor of ten — Class II is 0.5% of rated capacity, III is 0.1%, IV is 0.01%; Class V and VI are tiny measured amounts (ml/min) that depend on port size. Higher class = tighter, and harder to achieve and hold.

chapters.title: Fisher Easy-E Valve Maintenance
chapters.summary: The Fisher easy-e sliding-stem valve family end to end — what the trim does, how flow characteristic is set, which seals and packing to use, and the full disassemble / lap / repack / reassemble procedure.
objectives: List common trim components found in Fisher sliding-stem control valves
Identify types of sliding-stem valve bodies
Identify the inherent flow characteristic of cage and plug assemblies
Identify different types of packing used in control valves
Describe how to replace seal rings used with balanced plug assemblies
Describe the process for lapping metal-seated valves
Explain how to properly install and adjust packing

modules.title: Valve Bodies, Plugs & Seating
modules.objective: Identify Fisher sliding-stem valve body types and trim, and explain how balanced vs unbalanced plugs — and standard vs radius plug tips — differ.

keyConcepts.t: Trim is the set of parts in the flow path — plug, seat ring, cage, stem, and stem pin. The body is the pressure boundary; the bonnet closes the body, carries the packing, and keeps the plug aligned.
Globe and angle bodies run the same trim — an angle body just turns the flow path 90°.
Push-down-to-close (PDTC, direct-acting) vs push-down-to-open (PDTO, reverse-acting): which way stem travel drives the plug. This is what sets the assembly's fail action once an actuator is fitted.
A valve plug is the closure member. Two families — unbalanced and balanced — differing in whether process pressure acts on the whole plug face or is largely equalised.
Unbalanced plug: process pressure loads the full plug face — one seating leak path, tight shutoff, but a large actuator force. Standard flow is up through the seat ring.

Balanced plug: passages through the plug plus a piston (cage) seal equalise most of the static force — low stem force, but now two leak paths (seat and piston seal) and piston-seal temperature limits. Standard flow is down.

Metal seat, plug tip: a standard tip is a chamfered band lapped in to a matching seat ring — field-repairable by re-lapping. A radius tip is a rounded surface meeting a wide-bevel seat ring on a narrow line: Fisher's Class V metal construction on the easy-e (standard metal is Class IV). The concentrated line load seals tighter while the seat is true, but it tolerates damage poorly and is restored by re-machining, not lapping.

The seat ring is the plug's mating surface and part of the flow orifice. Metal seats take high temperature and are lapped; soft (PTFE-insert) seats give tighter shutoff at lower force; a wide-bevel metal seat is the partner to a radius plug.

modules.title: Plug Guiding, Cages & Flow Characteristics
modules.objective: Distinguish cage-guided from post-guided trim, explain the cage's three jobs, and explain how cage-window or formed-plug shape sets the inherent flow characteristic.

keyConcepts.t: Guiding keeps the plug aligned with its seat through the whole stroke. Two mechanisms: cage-guided — the plug rides in the cage bore; and post-guided — the plug rides on a post, with a seat ring retainer in place of a cage.

The cage does three jobs: guides the plug on a large bearing surface, clamps the seat ring in place, and — through its window shape — sets the flow characteristic. Cage-guided trim suits clean service, balanced or unbalanced.
Post-guided trim guides the plug on a post instead of a cage bore, for viscous, dirty or non-lubricating service where a close cage fit would foul (Fisher EZ).
Inherent flow characteristic = how the flow coefficient (Cv) changes with travel at a constant pressure drop. It is fixed by the trim geometry.

Three standard characteristics, set by cage-window shape — quick-opening: square windows, most Cv in the first part of travel, for on/off and dump. Linear: Cv proportional to travel, for constant-ΔP service. Equal percentage: each equal step of travel is an equal % change in Cv, the default where ΔP falls as flow rises.
A formed (contoured) plug can characterise flow on its own, without cage windows — used on post-guided valves like the EZ.

modules.title: easy-e Trim Seals & Packing
modules.objective: Match the easy-e valve types (ES / ED / ET / EZ) to their seals and shutoff classes, and select the right stem packing for the service.

keyConcepts.t: The easy-e family: ES (unbalanced, cage-guided, metal seat, Class IV); ED (balanced, cage-guided, graphite piston seal, Class II); ET (balanced, cage-guided, PTFE soft seat, Class V); EZ (unbalanced, post-guided, metal seat, Class IV). Class VI on any of them needs a soft/PTFE seat.
Piston-seal choice follows temperature: graphite piston rings for high temperature (ED); two-piece or spring-loaded PTFE for lower temperature (ET).
Packing seals along the stem, inside the packing box; the packing flange and nuts set its compression.

Stem packing by service — PTFE: low friction, below ~450 °F, spring-loaded or jam. Graphite: high temperature, high friction, jam or high-seal live-loaded. ENVIRO-SEAL: live-loaded for fugitive-emission limits, in PTFE, graphite ULF, or duplex.

modules.title: Body Disassembly & Seal Replacement
modules.objective: Disassemble an easy-e valve body safely, decide which trim parts can be reused, and replace the balanced-plug piston seal in its three easy-e forms — ED graphite ring, ET two-piece PTFE, and ET spring-loaded PTFE.

keyConcepts.t: Disassembly runs to a set order and is never rushed: isolate, depressurise both sides, drain, lock out. Pull the actuator, back off the packing-flange nuts, then loosen the body-to-bonnet nuts about 1/8 in and break the gasket joint by rocking or prying — a stuck bonnet is never freed by pulling with anything that can store and release energy. Match-mark actuator-to-bonnet and bonnet-to-body first so orientation and flow direction go back the same way; fit a stem locknut so the plug and stem cannot drop out of the lifting bonnet; lift from the far side.

Unbalanced plugs (ES, EZ) carry no piston seal, so their maintenance is minimal: verify the seating surface — lap minor defects, machine or replace gouges; a sound plug is reusable — and check the stem, polishing light thread defects and replacing it for gouges. Never put a new plug on an old stem: refitting needs a fresh pin hole, which weakens the stem enough to fail in service. A used plug on a new stem is fine. Stem surface damage also destroys new packing.

Balanced plugs seal at the plug OD against the cage bore. easy-e uses three seals: ED's graphite piston ring for high temperature, ET's two-piece PTFE with an elastomer backup ring, and ET's optional spring-loaded PTFE. The PTFE seals are pressure-assisted — the open (spring) side must face the process pressure, so the orientation flips with flow direction (open side down for flow-down, up for flow-up). Take the exact orientation from the manual figure for that seal.

The ED graphite piston ring is brittle and installs in pieces — two ideally, never more than three. A new ring comes whole: compress it into an oval in a smooth- or taped-jaw vise until it snaps on both sides; if one side goes first, keep squeezing rather than cutting the other. Fit the pieces in the plug groove with the broken ends matched — the mating fracture faces form the seal.

Both ET PTFE seals are stretched on slowly — PTFE needs time to cold-flow, so no sharp jerks — with silicone-base lubricant. The two-piece seal is a closed ring: cut it off, fit the backup ring then the seal; it looks loose in the groove until the cage squeezes it home. The spring-loaded seal on smaller plugs (5-3/8 in port or less) comes off and on with its spiral retaining clip and is reusable; on larger plugs it is cut off.

Reinstalling the plug is where a new seal gets ruined: lower it so the seal ring meets the cage's entrance chamfer squarely and enters evenly all the way round, never cocked. Inspect the plug groove and the cage bore for scratches first — a nick in either leaks past any new seal.

modules.title: Valve Lapping
modules.objective: Lap a metal-seated easy-e valve to a solid, even seating line; recognise when lapping is not the fix (radius seats, deep gouges, bellows-seal bonnets); and identify the plug and cage damage that poor lapping practice causes.

keyConcepts.t: Lapping works two mating metal seating surfaces against each other with an abrasive compound until they share one continuous contact band — the lap line. A solid, even line all the way round is both the goal and the pass/fail check; a broken or patchy line leaks. Lapping only cleans up minor surface defects — deep nicks and gouges are machined out or the part replaced, not lapped away.

Not every seat gets lapped. A radius (spherical) plug seats on a narrow line by design; lapping would spread that band and ruin the shutoff, so a damaged radius seat is re-machined, not lapped. Never lap an ENVIRO-SEAL bellows-seal bonnet — the bellows stops the stem turning and forcing it wrecks the bellows — and EZ Overtravel (EZ-OVT) trim is not lapped either.

Lap in a partial assembly so the trim holds the plug true: spread 280 to 600 grit compound on the seating surfaces, set the seat ring, install the cage — it clamps the seat ring and guides the plug — over a sacrificial old gasket, and bolt the bonnet down. The cage guiding keeps the plug square to the seat while it is worked.

Work the plug under its own weight only — no push — turning it back and forth through part of a turn with a handle on the stem. Every so often lift it clear, rotate 90 degrees, and carry on: this refreshes the compound and keeps wear even instead of cutting a groove. Then pull the plug, clean it, and read the lap line.

Once the lap line is solid and even, break the setup down, clean every trace of compound off the plug and seat ring, and reassemble the valve for real — new gaskets this time. Test for shutoff; if it still leaks too much, lap again.

Two mistakes ruin the trim. Lapping grit left behind is an abrasive — it galls and scores the plug and cage in service. A bonnet pulled down crooked or out of torque sequence cocks the cage, so the plug rubs and wears. Both are avoided the same way: clean completely and follow the torque procedure on final assembly.

modules.title: Packing Replacement & Adjustment
modules.objective: Remove and rebuild a valve's stem packing — spring-loaded and jam PTFE, jam graphite, HIGH-SEAL, and ENVIRO-SEAL — and set each one to its own correct compression method.

keyConcepts.t: Best practice is to pull the bonnet and push the old packing out the top with a non-marring rod — never work it out from below or gouge the packing bore. Then inspect the stem threads and the bore for burrs and scratches; light-sand what you can, replace what you cannot. A nick in the bore or on the stem leaks past new packing or cuts it on installation. The 20/20 rule gauges a used bore: usable if under 20% is pitted and no pit is deeper than 0.020 in.

Build the stack one ring at a time, seating each with the packing follower (a smooth pipe over the stem). Orientation matters: the male and female end adaptors face the right way and the lantern ring lines up with the lubricator / leak-off port. Which arrangement — single or double, and the ring count — comes from the valve manual for that stem diameter.

PTFE has two adjustment methods. Spring-loaded single V-ring is live-loaded: tighten the flange nuts evenly until the follower shoulder bottoms on the bonnet and the spring is compressed — the spring then holds the load. Jam (multi-ring) PTFE is torque-set: lubricate the studs and nut faces, tighten alternately to the minimum table torque with the follower clear of the bonnet, and leave the flange level and square to the stem.

Graphite rings (die-formed ribbon and braided filament, with a sacrificial zinc washer under each ribbon ring) go in one at a time, follower-seated, keeping air out of the box. Adjustment is two-step: torque to the maximum table value to crush the rings into the box, then back the nuts off and retighten to the minimum — this seats the packing without leaving it over-tight for running friction.

HIGH-SEAL is the higher pressure/temperature version of ENVIRO-SEAL — a long-travel Belleville spring pack with a load scale (D101453X012), and it is set by the scale, not by torque. Anti-seize the studs and nuts and hand-tighten; loosen the load-scale screws and line the bottom edge of the scale up with the indicator disk while the springs are still uncompressed; then tighten the nuts alternately and evenly, flange kept parallel, until the indicator disk reaches the maximum-compression line.

ENVIRO-SEAL is Belleville-loaded packing in double PTFE, single graphite ULF, or duplex, adjusted by the spring-flat method (D101642X012). Anti-seize the studs and nuts — threads and nut faces — hand-tighten, then tighten alternately and evenly, flange parallel, until the Belleville springs go 100% flat, shown by a sharp jump in nut torque. Then back each nut off to the 85% target load: 1/2 turn for PTFE or duplex, 1/4 turn for graphite ULF. The packing rings themselves are not lubricated.

modules.title: Reassembly & Gaskets
modules.objective: Reassemble an easy-e valve body with the right new gaskets in the right places, and torque the bonnet down by the correct method.

keyConcepts.t: A disturbed gasket is a dead gasket: any time a gasketed joint is opened, that gasket is replaced on reassembly, never reused. easy-e uses three kinds — thin graphite flat sheet for the bonnet and seat-ring joints, a metal shim to set stack height, and a spiral-wound gasket in the trim.

The spiral-wound gasket is a live element: it stays springy as the trim heats, expands and contracts, so it keeps the seat-ring gasket loaded and sealed through thermal cycling. The flat-sheet gaskets only seal a static joint.

The stack from the bottom up: seat ring on its gasket, then the cage, then the spiral-wound gasket and shim on top of the cage, then the bonnet gasket, then the bonnet. Bolting the bonnet down is one torque path that loads the seat-ring gasket, the spiral-wound gasket, and the body-to-bonnet joint together.

The bonnet is never pulled straight to final torque. Clean the stud threads, lubricate the bolting, align the match marks, then tighten the nuts crosswise in progressive steps — tightening one nut relaxes its neighbour, so you work round the pattern several times, stepping the torque up each round, until every nut holds the table value and the joint is sealed.

Bonnet studs and nuts are a rated part: use only the material on the valve's serial card — the wrong grade can be overstressed in service — and install each stud so its grade and maker's mark stay visible. Table torque values assume the specified lubricant (lithium-based grease); a dry or differently-lubed joint gives the wrong clamp load.

chapters.title: Sliding-Stem Spring & Diaphragm Actuator Maintenance
chapters.summary: Actuator action and fail mode, valve forces, bench set, and maintenance of the Fisher 657 and 667 actuators. Deadband.
objectives: Define the action of the actuator
Identify Fisher spring & diaphragm actuator types
Identify the fail mode of the control valve assembly
List valve forces that affect actuator operation and selection
Define bench set and describe the procedure for setting it
Describe common maintenance for the Fisher 657 and 667 actuators
Describe deadband as it applies to control valves

modules.title: Actuator Action, Fail Mode & Bench Set
modules.stakes: Choose the wrong actuator action or body orientation and the valve drives to the unsafe position on loss of air; misjudge bench set and the spring will not deliver rated travel or the seat load the shutoff class needs.
modules.objective: Determine a spring-and-diaphragm control valve assembly's fail mode from its actuator action and body orientation, and explain what bench set is and which valve forces it deliberately excludes.

keyConcepts.t: Actuator action is which way loading pressure drives the stem. Direct-acting (Fisher 657): air on top of the diaphragm pushes the stem down, the spring lifts it back up. Reverse-acting (Fisher 667): air lifts the stem up, the spring pushes it down.

Fail mode of the assembly is where the plug goes on loss of air. It is set by actuator action combined with body orientation (PDTC vs PDTO) — the same actuator can fail a valve open or closed depending on how the body is built.

Push-down-to-close (direct-acting) body: the plug sits between actuator and seat, stem extension seats the plug, and the seat ring is the lower travel stop. Push-down-to-open (reverse-acting) body: the seat ring sits between actuator and plug, stem extension opens the valve, and the seat ring is the upper travel stop.
Selecting an action: first decide whether the spring should open or close the valve on air failure, then choose actuator action and body orientation together to give that fail-safe result.

Bench set is the diaphragm-pressure range that strokes the actuator through the RATED valve travel with the assembly on the bench — no process or valve forces acting. The spring rate is chosen for the service conditions and the ANSI shutoff class wanted.

Bench set is defined friction-free: it deliberately excludes the in-service valve forces the actuator must also overcome — static plug unbalance (A), seat load (B), packing friction (C), and additional forces such as piston-ring friction (D).

modules.title: Fisher 657 — Identify & Bench Set
modules.stakes: A 657 set to the wrong bench set will not stroke to rated travel in service, and removing a diaphragm casing with spring compression still on it throws the cover off.
modules.objective: Identify a Fisher 657 direct-acting actuator from its construction and nameplate, and measure and set its bench set with the actuator off the valve.

keyConcepts.t: The 657 is a direct-acting, spring-opposed diaphragm actuator: loading pressure on top of the diaphragm pushes the stem down, the spring pushes it back up — so the stem fails up (retracts) on loss of air.

Construction top to bottom: upper and lower diaphragm casings with the diaphragm and diaphragm plate between them, the actuator spring below on its spring seat, and the spring adjuster threaded in the yoke to set initial spring compression.

The upper diaphragm casing holds the compressed spring's force. Thread the spring adjuster out until all spring compression is relieved before removing the casing cap screws, or the casing is thrown off.
Read the nameplate before working: actuator type and size, bench-set range (e.g. 3-11 psig), rated travel, and maximum valve stem diameter — these define what a correct bench set looks like.
Bench set is the initial spring compression, checked with the actuator off the valve so there is no packing friction. The lower bench-set pressure is where the actuator stem first moves.

To set and verify it: apply the lower bench-set pressure and mark the stem at first movement, then apply the upper bench-set pressure and measure the travel between marks — it must equal the rated travel on the nameplate.

modules.title: Fisher 657 — Mount & Service
modules.stakes: An actuator mounted with too little stem-connector thread engagement, or a diaphragm casing torqued out of sequence, strips threads, mis-sets travel, or leaks the diaphragm.
modules.objective: Mount a Fisher 657 actuator on a valve, set its travel, and disassemble and reassemble the diaphragm casing safely to the correct bolt torque.

keyConcepts.t: Before mounting, push the valve plug and stem down into the body, away from the actuator. The 657 spring holds its stem up; a raised valve stem fouls the mounting and can bend the stem or damage the threads.
Lift or hoist the actuator onto the bonnet and run the yoke locknut down against the bonnet, tightened with a hammer and blunt chisel. Do not connect the actuator and valve stems yet.

The stem connector must engage each stem — actuator and valve — by at least one stem diameter of thread; incomplete engagement strips threads or gives improper travel. Fine travel adjustment is at the locknut and jam nut.

With the actuator on the valve, re-check travel: stroke it and confirm full rated travel is reached by the upper bench-set value. Once packing friction is present, full travel occurs at bench set plus the friction force divided by the diaphragm area.

Disassembly order: bypass the valve, vent the loading pressure, then thread the spring adjuster out until all spring compression is relieved BEFORE removing the diaphragm-casing cap screws — a precompressed spring throws the upper casing off.

Reassembly torque: diaphragm-casing bolts go on clean and dry (no lubricant). Tighten four bolts 90 degrees apart, then criss-cross the rest, in two rounds — 13 N·m (10 lbf·ft) then 27 N·m (20 lbf·ft) — finishing with a circular check pass.

modules.title: Fisher 667 — Identify & Bench Set
modules.stakes: A 667 bench-set wrong fails to reach rated travel, and a nicked or dry seal-bushing O-ring makes the reverse-acting stem bind or leak.
modules.objective: Identify a Fisher 667 reverse-acting actuator and its fail-down spring action, and measure and set its bench set with the actuator off the valve.

keyConcepts.t: The 667 is a reverse-acting, spring-opposed diaphragm actuator: loading pressure lifts the stem up into the actuator and the spring pushes it down out of the yoke. Air enters at the yoke and follows an internal air path to the lower casing; the top casing is vented.

Because the spring pushes the stem down, a 667 connected to a valve drives the plug/stem assembly down and fails down on loss of air. Release the spring force before removing the stem connector or parts move suddenly.

The 667 actuator stem runs through a seal bushing carrying two O-rings in the yoke — the seal the 657 does not have. It must stroke smoothly; binding there points to wrong assembly or damaged O-rings.
Read the nameplate: actuator type and size, bench-set range (e.g. 7-15 psig), rated travel, and stem diameter.
Bench set is checked with the actuator off the valve so there is no packing friction. Adjust the spring adjuster until the stem first moves exactly at the nameplate bench-set pressure.

Off the valve, measure travel by the screwdriver method: hold a marked screwdriver or scale against the stem, mark it at the low bench-set pressure and again at the high bench-set pressure — the distance between marks is the actuator travel and must equal rated travel.

modules.title: Fisher 667 — Mount & Service
modules.stakes: Skipping spring-compression relief or getting the diaphragm-casing torque pattern wrong on a 667 damages the diaphragm, distorts the casing, or lets parts move under load.
modules.objective: Mount a Fisher 667 actuator on a valve, set its travel, and replace its spring, seal bushing, and diaphragm safely to the correct diaphragm casing torque.

keyConcepts.t: Mounting: push the valve plug and stem down into the body, apply air to retract (lift) the actuator stem clear, lift the actuator onto the bonnet, make sure the yoke seats against the bonnet, then tighten the yoke locknut with a hammer and blunt chisel.

Set travel on the valve: engage the stem connector at least one stem diameter of thread, apply full supply pressure and mark the stem at rated travel, then decrease diaphragm pressure and confirm rated travel is reached by the lower bench-set value (the 667 strokes opposite to the 657).

Removing the spring: with all spring compression relieved by the spring adjuster, the spring drops out the bottom of the spring barrel; it can then be used as a tool to drive the seal bushing out once the diaphragm and diaphragm plate are off.

Seal bushing: it carries the stem O-rings and comes out by removing its snap ring and pushing from the bottom. On reassembly, lubricate the O-rings and bushing with lithium grease and feed the stem threads through carefully so they do not cut the O-rings.
Diaphragm change-out: the diaphragm is installed between the upper and lower diaphragm plates, with the travel-stop spacer between the upper plate and the stem cap screw.

Diaphragm-casing bolt torque: bolts clean and dry; four bolts 90 degrees apart then diagonal/criss-cross, in two rounds — 13 N·m (10 lbf·ft) then 27 N·m (20 lbf·ft) — then verify in a circular pattern.

modules.title: Deadband
modules.stakes: Ignore deadband and the valve sits still while the signal changes — the loop hunts, offsets, or limit-cycles and the process never settles.
modules.objective: Explain deadband in a control valve assembly, what causes it, and how adding a positioner overcomes it.

keyConcepts.t: Deadband is the change in diaphragm pressure needed to reverse the valve's direction of travel — the input signal can move by that much with no stem response.
On the travel-vs-pressure graph it is the horizontal gap between the opening and closing curves: on a valve the actuator needs 'bench set plus deadband' pressure, not bench set alone, to move.
The cause is friction — mainly packing friction, plus unbalanced forces. Bench set is defined friction-free, so deadband is what real in-service friction adds on top of it.

Effect on control: every controller reversal is lost motion, giving sluggish response, offset, or limit cycling. A high-gain positioner drives the actuator through the deadband and largely removes it.
